'Whether you're a top or bottom it's all about consent'. Damn right 😊

1. Use freshly ground beef
2. Keep everything cold
3. Don’t handle your beef too much 
4. Don’t mix ingredients or salt into your patty 
5. Keep your patties consistent in size and weight
6. The shape of your patty matters - add a dimple to the center of your thick patties (just pressing with your thumb should work. For a thin patty, press with a flat surface to get an even thickness.
7. Season the outside with salt and pepper liberally
8. Use a two zone fire on your grill. Half your burners on high, half on low, so you can shift your patties around during cooking 
9. Make sure you get good browning on your beef 
10. Use a meat thermometer (120 for medium rare)
11. Choose your bun wisely. You need something heartier like brioche style for thicker burgers 
12. Do whatever you want with your toppings! 

I’ll add, and he did do this in the video, toast your buns to prevent them from getting soggy and to add more flavor. Also, make sure you have a clean grill, do not press on your patties with the spatula. Bit of a cheat code for doneness, if you see liquid pooling on the top of the patty, it’s time to flip, unless you’re looking for a well done patty. You can also season your toppings for extra flavor. Tomatoes with salt are better, so they’re better on burgers too.

So this video has stuck in my mind for a long time because of the whole "don't pre-salt the mix because you'll make it tough like meatloaf" thing.
As loathe as I am to disagree with Kenji, last night I deviated from my usual method (apply salt to ground beef, gently fold into the meat without kneading) to do what Kenji does, specifically very little handling, and salting the meat just before it goes in the pan.
I ended up with a patty that didn't stay together well, had a pretty boring texture, and was not evenly seasoned, resulting in a pretty bland and uninteresting burger, which is the complete opposite to how it usually comes out.

In the part of this video where he highlights the "shoot from a couple weeks ago" that give us the burger throwing clips, he kneads the meat for a full minute, perhaps even longer, and really gets his knuckles involved, even does some of that to a lesser extent in this video. This is not something I'd ever do, regardless of when I'm salting it. It really shouldn't be treated like this if you aren't making meatloaf, and pre-seasoning your burger absolutely does not need it. I feel like this is an unfair comparison, because nobody pre-salting their burger should be working it like this.

Then again, I like seasoned beef flavour, not just beef flavour, so that might be why I feel differently.

1.  Use Freshly Ground Beef: Opt for freshly ground beef, ideally from a butcher, for a loose, juicy texture. Avoid compressed, pre-packaged beef which can be tougher and less flavorful.
2.  Keep Everything Cold: Keep beef cold to maintain solid fat chunks, which enhances flavor. Avoid letting it sit out too long before forming patties.
3.  Handle Meat Gently: Form patties quickly and lightly to avoid overworking the meat, which can make it tough like sausage. Use parchment paper to shape without excessive handling.
4.  Season After Forming Patties: Avoid mixing salt or other ingredients into the beef before forming patties to prevent toughness. Season only the outside after shaping.
5.  Ensure Consistent Patty Size: Use a scale for uniform patties to ensure even cooking over the same heat.
6.  Shape Patties Thoughtfully: For thick patties, create a dimple in the center to prevent bulging during cooking. For thin patties, press between parchment paper for an even shape.
7.  Season Liberally: Use kosher salt and black pepper generously on the outside to enhance beef flavor, as salt is critical for taste.
8.  Use a Two-Zone Fire: Set up a grill with a hot side and a cooler side to control cooking, prevent flare-ups, and allow precise doneness for thicker burgers.
9.  Achieve Good Browning: Prioritize browning for flavor via the Maillard reaction. For thick burgers, brown both sides; for thin burgers, focus on one side to avoid drying out.
10.  Use a Thermometer: Check doneness with a thermometer (120°F for medium-rare, 130°F for upper medium-rare, 160°F for well-done) for accuracy, especially for occasional cooks.
11.  Choose the Right Bun: Use soft white buns for thin burgers and sturdier brioche-style buns for thick, juicy burgers to prevent sogginess.
12.  Personalize Toppings: Toppings are a personal choice—use what you like, whether simple (onions, pickles) or loaded (lettuce, tomato). Place toppings above or below the patty based on preference.

Don't forget to clean your grill before and after. After to remove the bits that may attract bugs, and then before can just be a swipe of an oiled paper towel using tongs while the grate is hot that will help keep food from sticking. 
Absolutely do not use wire grill brushes to clean your grill! The wires come loose and can lodge in your food and stick in or perforate your mouth to your gut. Instead use spiraled metal, nylon, chainmail, pumice, etc. - there are many alternatives that will be right for your grill surface.
